parameters.Features: Thermal Protection;Short-Circuit  Protection;Overvoltage protection;Data encryption;Built-in signature detection

pins.name: MISO
pins.source: inferred - by elimination, the only mandatory SPI signal left unexposed on the twelfth pad. Not stated by WIZnet. Settle it with a continuity check before soldering the module down.

provenance.pins: EasyEDA Pro symbol WIZ850IO read with tools/eda.py (pin numbers); datasheet p.2 Pin Description, J1 and J2 tables (names and types). The J2 header maps 12->7, NOT 7->12: all six names agree on that direction and none on the other. The symbol spells pin 5 SCNn; the datasheet says SCSn and the name here follows the datasheet.

designVerdict: SELECTED as the footprint reference for U3. The board is drawn to this pin map; the intended purchase is a cheaper W5500 Lite clone whose silkscreen has been read and matches.
notes: The design switched from a bare W5500 (C32843) to a soldered-down module. That retired two blocking open questions outright: the 25 MHz crystal's CL mismatch (18 pF required, 20 pF on hand) and the HR911105A centre-tap bias network that the W5500 datasheet does not document. Both are the module vendor's problem now.

CLONE ON HAND MATCHES THIS FOOTPRINT. Silkscreen read by the user as J1 = INT/CS/SCK/MO/G/G and J2 = G/V/V/NC/RST/WT; the user confirms J1 was read right-to-left. That is what reading both headers left-to-right across the board produces, since J1 and J2 sit on opposite edges and therefore run in opposite directions - so both readings are consistent with this record's map. J2 position 4 being NC independently confirms WIZ850io-class rather than WIZ550io, which carries RDY there.

'WT' IS MISO, BY ELIMINATION rather than by datasheet. Twelve pads total; eleven are identified (3x GND, 2x 3V3, NC, RSTn, INT, CS, SCK, MO) and the only mandatory SPI signal left unexposed is MISO - a W5500 module without it would be useless. It also sits in the position both official variants use for MISO. This is provenance 'inferred', NOT datasheet-read: weaker than the rest of this map, and worth a continuity check against the W5500 before the board is ordered.

HANDEDNESS CANNOT BE SETTLED ON PAPER. WIZnet's wiki carries a pinmap image and links an external dimension PDF; the LCSC datasheet is an export of that page. Neither states which physical end is pin 1, so whether a clone is a mirror of the official footprint is not a documentary question. Resolve it with a multimeter: all grounds are common, so ringing J2 position 1 against the two G pads on J1 identifies J1's ground end, which with the silkscreen signal order fixes the orientation. Then label every pad on the controller's silkscreen so a mirrored module is caught by reading one silkscreen against the other before soldering.

'HanRun HR961160C' is the marking on the RJ45 JACK, not the module. HanRun makes the jacks (HR911105A is the same family), so that number identifies the connector and cannot identify which W5500 board it is fitted to.

PRICE: $22.89 at LCSC against roughly $3-6 for a clone and $4.65 for the discrete chip + crystal + jack it replaces. Buying official costs about five times the discrete BOM for this block, which is why the clone is the intended purchase and this record exists as the documented reference.
INTn (J1-6) is typed 'I' in the datasheet's own pin table, which is wrong - it is the W5500's open-drain interrupt OUTPUT. Recorded here as open_collector.

RSTn needs LOW for at least 500 us, and firmware must wait 50 ms after it returns HIGH before talking to the module (p.2). The controller keeps the pull-down that holds the PHY in reset while the MCU boots.

AREA IS NOT A WIN: 25 x 23 mm = 575 mm2 against roughly 496 mm2 for the parts it replaces, so the board gets slightly bigger. The win is the retired open questions, six retired exact values and the differential routing.

Not a JLCPCB assembly part - fitted by hand like the picoMAX connectors. Soldered down rather than socketed, because this is a soundwall and a stacked daughterboard on a receptacle is the connection that works loose.

PIN KEYS ARE NOT PAD NUMBERS. The map is keyed J1-1..J2-6 after the module's own silkscreen. A netlist keys "pins" by pad number, so these keys cannot be used directly and K3-unknown-pin would fire on all twelve. The EasyEDA symbol's pad numbering has to be read off the library part before the netlist is written - and is not knowable from the datasheet.
The J1/J2 naming also collides with this board's own J1 (USB-C) and J2/J3 (picoMAX). Keep the module's designations inside this record and never in design prose.
erc.py has no per-pin provenance: unverified() matches provenance.pins against the whole string, so the MISO caveat above does NOT downgrade severity. Treated at full confidence by the checker today.
